ndvi.title: NDVI (plant greenness)
ndvi.text: Satellites measure how green the ground looks, from 0 (bare dirt) to 1 (thick green crop). We count a month below 0.25 as bare, above 0.40 as green, and in between as partly covered.

soilMoisture.title: Soil moisture anomaly
soilMoisture.text: How wet or dry the root zone was in the growing season compared with this field’s normal, from NASA’s SMAP satellite (each reading covers about 7 miles). −28% means 28% drier than normal. SMAP starts in 2015, so earlier years use rain instead.

hydrologicGroup.title: Hydrologic group
hydrologicGroup.text: How fast rain soaks into your soil. Group A soaks in fastest. Group D is slowest, so more rain runs off the field.

coverCrop.title: Cover crop
coverCrop.text: A crop grown mainly to protect and feed the soil between cash crops, like cereal rye or hairy vetch.

slope.title: Slope
slope.text: How steep your field is. On steeper ground, rain washes soil away faster. Measured from a NASA elevation map.

confidence.title: Confidence
confidence.text: High, medium or low. A rotation gains points for 30 or more years of weather data, 8 or more years of crop maps, crops that have grown on your field before, a crop model that was right on years it never saw (balanced accuracy of 70% or more), and two rain datasets that agree. It loses points for crops that are new to the field, crops satellites struggle to recognize, and crop traits that are only estimates. Data detail (30 m maps vs. weather averaged over about 30 miles) adds no points. We state it so nobody over-reads it.

score.title: Score
score.text: A number from 0 to 100 for how well a rotation fits your goals and limits. Your chosen goals count double. Every rule is open for experts to check.

bareDays.title: Bare days
bareDays.text: Estimated days a year when satellites would see little or no plant cover, so the soil is open to wind and rain. Based on Landsat 8 and 9 years from 2014 on (see “Why 2013 matters”), your field’s own crop history where we have it, and regional patterns for the rest.

heldOut.title: Tested on unseen years
heldOut.text: We trained each model only on years before 2023, then checked its answers once for 2023, 2024 and 2025, years it had never seen. That shows how it does on a year like next year. Overall accuracy is how often it was right. Balanced accuracy averages the right-rate for each crop, so common crops can't hide trouble with rarer ones. Guessing “same as last year” is the bar to beat.

bareScore.title: Ground cover score
bareScore.text: 100 minus the share of the year the ground was bare. 100 means plants or residue all year. Lower means more bare days, when soil can wash or blow away.

ndti.title: NDTI and crop residue
ndti.text: NDTI is a satellite index that is supposed to spot dead crop stalks (residue) left on a field. We tested it, and a bare-soil index (BSI), on North Texas clay soils. They mostly reflect soil type and could not tell residue from bare dirt. So we do not claim to measure residue. We say “partly covered” for months between bare and green.

evapotranspiration.title: Evapotranspiration (ET)
evapotranspiration.text: Water that leaves a field as vapor, from the soil and from plants. NASA’s MODIS satellite estimates it. It predicted plant stress better in our tests, but MODIS builds ET partly from leaf greenness, so it would partly be answering with the answer. We left it out of every score.

frost.title: Frost risk and frost-free days
frost.text: Frost-free days are the days between the last freeze in spring and the first freeze in fall (a low of 32°F or colder). The frost dates on your field page come from PRISM (4 km, from weather stations): the middle date of the last 10 years. Greenline's year-pattern model uses NASA POWER's frost-free days, which run about 3 days longer on average. They set planting windows and decide whether a cool-season cover crop can finish. Greenline doesn't score frost risk for a rotation yet.

waterBalance.title: Water balance
waterBalance.text: Rain coming in compared with the water a crop needs over its season. Greenline compares each crop’s seasonal water need (from FAO) with this field’s rain and its dry years. It is a simple comparison, not a full soil-water model.

satVsGround.title: Satellite vs. ground measurements
satVsGround.text: Satellites see a whole region at once, every few days, for decades. But each reading is an average over a square (30 m for greenness, about 7 miles for soil moisture, about 30 miles for NASA POWER weather), and clouds can hide the ground. A rain gauge or soil probe measures one spot very well but only that spot. Neither is perfect, so we compare them where we can, such as satellite rain against ground-station rain (PRISM). Your own eyes and records on your field still count most.

sensor2013.title: Why 2013 matters
sensor2013.text: Landsat 7 sees plant greenness lower than Landsat 8 and 9, by about 0.05 NDVI on the same field and month. With a fixed cutoff for “bare”, that alone adds bare days. So every bare-day number here uses Landsat 8 and 9 only, from 2014 on. Years before 2013 had only the older satellites. We show them, marked low confidence, but don't use them in scores. Older years are still used for rain and heat history.

prism.title: Ground-station rain (PRISM)
prism.text: PRISM (Oregon State University) maps rain on a 4 km grid from thousands of rain gauges and weather stations. We use it to check NASA's rain data. We checked across 201 North Texas sample points, 2008–2024: yearly rain from NASA POWER matched PRISM with a correlation of 0.92 and read about 9% low; GPM IMERG matched at 0.93 and read about 4% high. Both NASA datasets are partly adjusted with gauge data, so this shows consistency, not fully independent proof. It doesn't change the confidence points.

kFactor.title: Erosion risk (K factor)
kFactor.text: How easily rain washes away your topsoil, from the USDA soil survey. It runs from about 0.02 to 0.69. Under 0.20 is low, 0.20 to 0.35 moderate, over 0.35 high. Greenline multiplies K by your slope: when K × slope is 0.5 or more (for example K 0.25 on a 2% slope), bare days cost more in the erosion score.

tFactor.title: Tolerable soil loss (T)
tFactor.text: The most soil, in tons per acre a year, that can wash or blow away while the field stays productive long term. From the USDA soil survey, 1 to 5. Deep soils get 5. It's a limit to stay under, not a measurement of what's lost now.

waterStorage.title: Water the soil holds
waterStorage.text: How much water plants can pull from the top 1 meter (3.3 ft) of soil when it's full, from the USDA soil survey. More storage carries crops through dry spells. Greenline uses it in the water score: under 4 in, thirsty crops lose more in drought-prone fields; 6 in or more, a little less.

landCapability.title: Land capability class
landCapability.text: The USDA's 1 to 8 rating of how suited land is to crops without irrigation. Class 1 has the fewest limits; class 5 and up are mostly for grass or trees. The letter says what limits it: e erosion, w wetness, s soil (shallow, stony or droughty), c climate. Shown for context; it isn't in the score.

grossRevenue.title: Gross revenue (dollar estimate)
grossRevenue.text: County yield × Texas price, averaged over 2021–2025, from the USDA NASS Quick Stats survey. It's money in before any costs (seed, fertilizer, fuel, rent), so it is not profit. When NASS doesn't publish your county's yield, we use the regional or Texas average and say so. Texas averages include irrigated High Plains farms and may run high for dryland North Texas. Dollars never change the score or the order of options.

fieldShiftModels.title: Field Shift study models
fieldShiftModels.text: Three models trained on 300 Ellis County fields. The crop classifier reads each year's satellite greenness curve and names the crop. It learned only from fields where most of the field had the same USDA crop label, and was tested on 2023–2025, years it never saw. The crop stress model predicts whether a field will be browner than its own normal next month, from weather, soil moisture and the field's recent past. It uses only earlier observations, so it can't peek at the answer. The year-type finder groups past seasons by rain, heat and soil wetness. With only 41 seasons, the groups overlap.

seasonReplay.title: Season replay
seasonReplay.text: We plant each rotation on paper and run it day by day through every real season since 1985, using NASA weather. A daily water balance tracks soil water, published crop factors turn water stress into yield, and the RUSLE formula estimates soil loss. For 2040 we shift those real seasons by the change that eight NASA climate models project. Each rotation is then graded on soil cover, erosion, profit, bad-year resilience, nitrogen and pests. It is a simulation built on published farm science, not a trained model, and a starting point for a talk with your Extension agent, not a prescription.

fieldShift.title: Ellis County season replay
fieldShift.intro: A study on {n} Ellis County fields: seven rotations replayed day by day through every season from 1985 to 2025 and through 2040 climate projections, then graded on six goals. It uses one typical field and one weather point, so it doesn't change your field's scores above.
fieldShift.keepLabel: Best in this study: keep it
fieldShift.scoreRank: {score} of 100 in today's climate · ranks {rank} of {of}
fieldShift.scoreWins: {score} of 100 in today's climate · best in {wins} of {of} scenarios
fieldShift.closeCall: Close call: {other} is only {gap} points behind.
fieldShift.tableCaption: Today's common rotation compared with the best rotation in the study

fieldShift.eqip: May qualify for about ${usd}/acre a year from NRCS EQIP for 3 years. Not counted in the grade; applications are competitive.
fieldShift.m1Line: right {clean}% of the time on years it never saw (2023–2025) for fields with one clear USDA crop label, {all}% on all fields.
fieldShift.m2Line: right {acc}% of the time on unseen years 2023–2025 (AUC {auc}), using only past observations.
fieldShift.m3Line: 1985–2025 seasons sorted into {drought} drought, {hot} hot, {normal} normal and {wet} wet years. Soft groups, a guide only.
fieldShift.notYourField: The replay is a simulation built on published agronomy (FAO-56 water balance, FAO-33 yield response, RUSLE soil loss), not machine learning. Prices, budgets and cost-share rates are estimates to check with your county Extension and NRCS office.
